lede: A motorsport digital twin and race-strategy research platform built around Sepang International Circuit. You do not drive the car. You act as the race engineer.

facts.label: Stack
facts.value: React Three Fiber · FastAPI · scikit-learn · MediaPipe

sections.headline: A strategy workstation, not a racing game.

body: Sepang Vision Lab puts an interactive digital twin of Sepang next to the tools a strategist would want: historical replay, telemetry, lap-time models, pit-strategy and Monte Carlo simulation, weather scenarios, webcam hand tracking and an AI race engineer.

It is deliberately not a driving game, a fantasy manager or a chatbot with racing trivia. The question it explores is how far honest, public race data can go before you have to start guessing, and how to show clearly where that line is.

Race strategy is made from partial information: lap times, gaps, pit windows, weather that might arrive. Public data covers only a slice of it. There is timing, but no pedal telemetry, no tyre compounds and no car positions between timing lines.

Most visualisations fill those gaps quietly with plausible-looking numbers. I wanted a system that used what the data actually supports, modelled what it could, and labelled everything else as an assumption.
Each capability depends on the one before it, so the project was built strictly in that order. No layer started until the one beneath it worked and was tested.

Sepang Vision Lab is under construction. These are captures of the current local build on the 2017 Malaysian Grand Prix timing archive. Movement is interpolated between timing lines, not GPS, and the screens say so.

items.caption: Historical workspace at lap 35: the 3D circuit, every car with timing coverage, the selected driver and the replay controls.
Tyre and stint analysis: an observed pace trend with its limits stated beside it.
Lap-time ML: the previous-lap baseline beats every trained model on test error, and the panel says so.

value.label: Sepang Vision Lab architecture
value.caption: No external calls happen during replay. The frontend never reads the raw API JSON directly.

nodes.title: Jolpica F1 API
nodes.detail: Ergast-compatible results, laps and pit stops.

nodes.title: Ingest
nodes.detail: Paginated, paced, cached. Validates lap sequences and the winner’s total time.

nodes.title: Parquet cache
nodes.detail: Raw-response hashes and retrieval time kept as provenance.

nodes.title: FastAPI
nodes.detail: Pydantic-validated replay, models and strategy endpoints.

nodes.title: Digital twin
nodes.detail: React Three Fiber scene; readouts refresh at 10 Hz.

nodes.title: Race engineer
nodes.detail: Selects drivers, seeks the race, branches strategies.

items.title: Circuit geometry
items.detail: Community GeoJSON, cross-checked against the operator’s circuit map. The projected path is ~5,549 m against a published 5.543 km (0.11% over). Smoothed with a centripetal Catmull–Rom spline.

items.title: Historical replay
items.detail: Cars move by linear reconstruction between recorded lap crossings. It is not GPS, and it is labelled that way. A retired car is never extrapolated around the track.

body: The lap-time experiment predicts lap N from the three previous laps, the lap number and the last recorded position. Splits are chronological across the whole field (train by 45 min, validate to 65 min, test after), so no model ever sees the future.
Random Forest won on validation MAE and was selected. On the test window it did not beat the naive previous-lap baseline, and the app says so prominently instead of hiding it.

value.caption: Lap-time models · 2017 Malaysian GP · chronological split (448 / 207 / 275 examples)
value.columns: Model | Validation MAE (s) | Test MAE (s) | Test RMSE (s) | Test R²
value.note: Single race only; not validated on unseen races.

items.title: Stint pace
items.detail: Median-of-pairwise-slopes regression per stint. Pit laps and the following lap are excluded but stay visible. Tyre-only degradation is reported as not identifiable from this data.

items.title: Monte Carlo
items.detail: 1,000–10,000 seeded scenarios per comparison. Every strategy shares the same random draws (common random numbers), so the differences come from the strategy, not the noise.

items.title: Strategy Lab
items.detail: Freezes a hypothetical branch from a driver’s last completed lap and compares stay out, pit now and a delayed stop. All defaults are editable and labelled illustrative.

items.title: Weather Lab
items.detail: Dry → light rain → wet → drying, with five deterministic tyre plans (slicks, early or delayed inters, early or delayed wets) and editable per-lap penalties.

items.title: Hand tracking
items.detail: MediaPipe HandLandmarker runs locally in a web worker, capped at 15 fps. No camera request is made until the user explicitly enables it.

items.title: AI race engineer
items.detail: The model may call exactly one tool, which re-runs the captured comparison. It cannot change inputs, and only simulator-derived numbers are shown. The no-AI path is labelled no-AI.

value.caption: Project cover. Concept artwork, not an interface capture.

body: Still open: the gesture model is waiting on real labelled recordings, and the live AI race-engineer path still needs end-to-end verification. Both are marked as open in the project rather than shown as finished.

items.title: Beat the naive model first
items.detail: A previous-lap guess outperformed every trained model on test. Showing that is more useful than a flattering chart.

items.title: Label the unknown
items.detail: Saying “tyre degradation is not identifiable here” is a finding, not a gap.

items.title: Layers keep you honest
items.detail: Building strictly bottom-up meant every new feature stood on something already tested.

items.title: Give AI a narrow job
items.detail: Letting the model explain the simulator, but never invent numbers, made the AI feature trustworthy.
